name: Chapter 12: Linear Programming
description: Linear programming problems, constraints, feasible region, corner point method, unbounded, infeasible and multiple-optimum cases, formulating word problems, with every answer computed.

cards.term: What is a linear programming problem (LPP)?
cards.definition: Finding the maximum or minimum of a linear objective function Z = ax + by subject to linear inequality constraints (and x, y ≥ 0). “Linear” because all relations are linear; “programming” means finding a plan of action

cards.term: Define objective function, constraints, decision variables.
cards.definition: Objective function: the linear expression Z = ax + by to be optimised. Constraints: the linear inequalities (or equations) on the variables. Decision variables: x and y, with the non-negative restrictions x, y ≥ 0

cards.term: Define feasible region, feasible and infeasible solutions.
cards.definition: Feasible region: the common region satisfying all constraints including x, y ≥ 0. Feasible solution: any point in (or on the boundary of) it. Infeasible: any point outside. Optimal solution: a feasible point giving the optimal value of Z

cards.term: What is a corner point (vertex) of the feasible region?
cards.definition: A point of the region that is the intersection of two boundary lines. The region is always convex (a convex polygon, bounded or not)

cards.term: Bounded vs unbounded feasible region?
cards.definition: Bounded: it can be enclosed in a circle. Unbounded: it extends indefinitely in some direction

cards.term: Theorem 1 of LPP (fundamental).
cards.definition: If Z has an optimal value (max or min) on the feasible region R, it occurs at a corner point of R

cards.term: Theorem 2 of LPP.
cards.definition: If R is bounded, Z has both a maximum and a minimum on R, and each occurs at a corner point. If R is unbounded an optimum may not exist

cards.term: Steps of the corner point method.
cards.definition: 1) Graph the constraints and find the feasible region and its corners. 2) Evaluate Z at each corner; let M be the largest, m the smallest. 3) If R is bounded, M is the max and m the min. 4) If R is unbounded: M is the max only if ax + by > M has no common point with R; m is the min only if ax + by < m has none; otherwise there is no such optimum

cards.term: Remark: multiple optimal solutions?
cards.definition: If two corner points give the same optimal value, then every point on the line segment joining them gives that value too (infinitely many optimal solutions)

cards.term: Types of outcomes of an LPP.
cards.definition: Unique optimum (one corner); multiple optima (an edge); unbounded (no max or no min); infeasible (no feasible region)

cards.term: How to graph a constraint like 3x + 5y ≤ 15.
cards.definition: Draw the line 3x + 5y = 15 through (5, 0) and (0, 3). Test the origin: 0 ≤ 15 is true, so shade the origin side. For a ≥ constraint through the origin, use another test point

cards.term: Why is the feasible region of an LPP convex?
cards.definition:
It is the intersection of half-planes, and each half-plane is convex.
This is why optimal values occur at corners (a linear function on a convex polygon is extreme at a vertex)

cards.term: The furniture dealer problem: mathematical formulation.
cards.definition: Let x tables and y chairs. Maximise Z = 250x + 75y subject to 2500x + 500y ≤ 50 000 (i.e. 5x + y ≤ 100), x + y ≤ 60, x, y ≥ 0

cards.term: Corner point method: evaluate Z at the vertices
cards.definition: Optimal value of Z = ax+by over a bounded feasible polygon occurs at a corner point; evaluate Z at each vertex; furniture dealer: max 250x+75y at (10,50) = 6250

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Corner point method

Maximise Z = 250x + 75y subject to 5x + y ≤ 100, x + y ≤ 60, x, y ≥ 0. Where does the maximum occur?

Find the vertices of the feasible region and evaluate Z at each.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Corner point method

Maximise Z = 250x + 75y subject to 5x + y ≤ 100, x + y ≤ 60, x, y ≥ 0. Where does the maximum occur?

The feasible region is the polygon OABC. Theorem: an optimal value of a linear objective over a convex polygon occurs at a corner point. So evaluate Z at O(0, 0), A(20, 0), B(10, 50), C(0, 60): 0, 5000, 6250, 4500.

The maximum profit ₹6250 is at B: buy 10 tables and 50 chairs. B is the intersection of 5x + y = 100 and x + y = 60 (subtract: 4x = 40).

cards.term: Iso-profit line touches the last vertex
cards.definition: Lines 3x+4y=c move across the region; maximum Z is at the last vertex touched, (0,4) with Z=16; corner values 0, 12, 16

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Iso-profit lines

Maximise Z = 3x + 4y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x, y ≥ 0. Slide the line 3x + 4y = c across the feasible region: where is it last touching?

Move the objective line parallel to itself.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Iso-profit lines

Maximise Z = 3x + 4y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x, y ≥ 0. Slide the line 3x + 4y = c across the feasible region: where is it last touching?

Each line 3x + 4y = c is a set of points with the same Z. As c increases the line moves up and to the right; the largest c for which it still meets the feasible triangle is when it just touches a corner: here (0, 4) with Z = 16.

Check with corner values: (0, 0) → 0, (4, 0) → 12, (0, 4) → 16 (Ex 12.1 Q1). Steeper or flatter objective lines would end at a different vertex.

cards.term: Example 1: maximise Z = 4x + y subject to x + y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 90, x, y ≥ 0.
Example 2: minimise Z = 200x + 500y subject to x + 2y ≥ 10, 3x + 4y ≤ 24, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Bounded triangle with corners (0, 5), (4, 3), (0, 6): Z = 2500, 3000, 2300. Minimum Z = 2300 at (4, 3)

cards.term: Two corners with the same optimum ⇒ the whole edge is optimal
cards.definition: If two corner points give the same optimal value, every point on the segment joining them is also optimal; Example 3: Z=3x+9y max 180 on segment CD (parallel to x+3y=60), min 60 at (5,5)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 3 · multiple optimal solutions

Minimise and maximise Z = 3x + 9y subject to x + 3y ≤ 60, x + y ≥ 10, x ≤ y, x, y ≥ 0. Why does the maximum occur at two corners?

Compare the slope of the objective line with the edges.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 3 · multiple optimal solutions

Minimise and maximise Z = 3x + 9y subject to x + 3y ≤ 60, x + y ≥ 10, x ≤ y, x, y ≥ 0. Why does the maximum occur at two corners?

Corner values: A(0, 10) → 90, B(5, 5) → 60, C(15, 15) → 180, D(0, 20) → 180. Minimum 60 at B. Maximum 180 at both C and D.

The objective line 3x + 9y = 180 is the same line as the constraint x + 3y = 60, so it contains the whole edge CD. Every point of segment CD is optimal: infinitely many solutions.

cards.term: Example 3: minimise and maximise Z = 3x + 9y subject to x + 3y ≤ 60, x + y ≥ 10, x ≤ y, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Corners A(0, 10), B(5, 5), C(15, 15), D(0, 20): Z = 90, 60, 180, 180. Min 60 at (5, 5); max 180 at every point of segment CD

cards.term: Unbounded feasible region: test the open half-plane
cards.definition: For an unbounded region, corner minimum m is the true minimum iff the open half-plane ax+by<m has no common point with the feasible region; example -50x+20y has no minimum

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 4 · unbounded region

Minimise Z = −50x + 20y over the unbounded region 2x − y ≥ −5, 3x + y ≥ 3, 2x − 3y ≤ 12, x, y ≥ 0. The smallest corner value is −300 at (6, 0). Is that the minimum?

Draw the half-plane Z < −300 and see whether it overlaps the region.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 4 · unbounded region

Minimise Z = −50x + 20y over the unbounded region 2x − y ≥ −5, 3x + y ≥ 3, 2x − 3y ≤ 12, x, y ≥ 0. The smallest corner value is −300 at (6, 0). Is that the minimum?

For an unbounded region the smallest corner value m is the minimum only if the open half-plane ax + by < m has no point in common with the region. Here −50x + 20y < −300, i.e. −5x + 2y < −30, does contain feasible points (the red wedge).

So Z can be made smaller than −300: Z has no minimum. Similarly, to check the maximum 100 at (0, 5) test −50x + 20y > 100: it also meets the region (large y), so no maximum either.

cards.term: Example 4: is the corner value −300 the minimum of Z = −50x + 20y on the unbounded region?
cards.definition: No: the half-plane −50x + 20y < −300 meets the region, so Z has no minimum. Likewise 100 at (0, 5) is not the maximum since −50x + 20y > 100 also meets the region

cards.term: Infeasible LPP: empty feasible region
cards.definition: If the constraints have no common point the feasible region is empty and the LPP has no solution; example x+y>=8 with 3x+5y<=15; Ex 12.1 Q10 also infeasible

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 5 · no feasible region

Minimise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≥ 8, 3x + 5y ≤ 15, x, y ≥ 0. What can you say?

Do the two shaded half-planes overlap anywhere?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 5 · no feasible region

Minimise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≥ 8, 3x + 5y ≤ 15, x, y ≥ 0. What can you say?

The half-plane x + y ≥ 8 lies on the far side of its line; 3x + 5y ≤ 15 is the small triangle near the origin. They have no point in common (even the largest x + y in the triangle is 5 < 8), so the feasible region is empty and the problem has no solution.

Same happens in Ex 12.1 Q10: x − y ≤ −1 means y ≥ x + 1 while −x + y ≤ 0 means y ≤ x. An LPP can therefore be infeasible, unbounded with or without an optimum, or have a unique / multiple optimum.

cards.term: Example 5: minimise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≥ 8, 3x + 5y ≤ 15, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: No feasible region, hence no feasible solution (the two half-planes do not overlap)

cards.term: Ex 12.1 Q1: maximise Z = 3x + 4y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Corners: (0, 0) → 0; (0, 4) → 16; (4, 0) → 12. Maximum Z = 16 at (0, 4)

cards.term: Ex 12.1 Q2: minimise Z = −3x + 4y subject to x + 2y ≤ 8, 3x + 2y ≤ 12, x, y ≥ 0.
Ex 12.1 Q3: maximise Z = 5x + 3y subject to 3x + 5y ≤ 15, 5x + 2y ≤ 10, x, y ≥ 0.
Ex 12.1 Q4: minimise Z = 3x + 5y subject to x + 3y ≥ 3, x + y ≥ 2, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Unbounded region, corners: (0, 2) → 10; (3/2, 1/2) → 7; (3, 0) → 9. The smallest is 7; the half-plane 3x + 5y < 7 has no point in common with the region, so minimum Z = 7 at (3/2, 1/2)

cards.term: Ex 12.1 Q5: maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + 2y ≤ 10, 3x + y ≤ 15, x, y ≥ 0.
Ex 12.1 Q6: minimise Z = x + 2y subject to 2x + y ≥ 3, x + 2y ≥ 6, x, y ≥ 0. Show the minimum occurs at more than two points.
cards.definition: Corners: (0, 3) → 6; (6, 0) → 6. Both give 6, and the objective line x + 2y = 6 is the edge x + 2y ≥ 6. Minimum Z = 6 at every point of the segment joining (0, 3) and (6, 0)

cards.term: Ex 12.1 Q7: minimise and maximise Z = 5x + 10y subject to x + 2y ≤ 120, x + y ≥ 60, x − 2y ≥ 0, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Corners: (40, 20) → 400; (60, 0) → 300; (60, 30) → 600; (120, 0) → 600. Minimum Z = 300 at (60, 0); maximum Z = 600 at (120, 0) and (60, 30) and all points on the segment between them (the objective line is parallel to x + 2y = 120)

cards.term: Ex 12.1 Q8: minimise and maximise Z = x + 2y subject to x + 2y ≥ 100, 2x − y ≤ 0, 2x + y ≤ 200, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Corners: (0, 50) → 100; (0, 200) → 400; (20, 40) → 100; (50, 100) → 250. Minimum Z = 100 at every point of the segment joining (0, 50) and (20, 40); maximum Z = 400 at (0, 200)

cards.term: Ex 12.1 Q9: maximise Z = −x + 2y subject to x ≥ 3, x + y ≥ 5, x + 2y ≥ 6, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Unbounded region with corners: (3, 2) → 1; (4, 1) → -2; (6, 0) → -6. The corner maximum is 1, but −x + 2y > 1 has points in the region (take y large). Z has no maximum value

cards.term: Ex 12.1 Q10: maximise Z = x + y subject to x − y ≤ −1, −x + y ≤ 0, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: x − y ≤ −1 gives y ≥ x + 1, while −x + y ≤ 0 gives y ≤ x. These cannot both hold: no feasible region, so no maximum

cards.term: Formulating an LPP from words: method.
cards.definition: 1) Name the decision variables x, y. 2) Write the objective (profit, cost) as Z = ax + by. 3) Turn each limit (time, money, space, ingredients) into a linear inequality: “at most” → ≤, “at least” → ≥. 4) Add x, y ≥ 0. 5) Solve by corner points

cards.term: Production plan: a factory makes products P and Q. Machine time: 2x + y ≤ 100; labour: x + y ≤ 80; demand for P at most 40. Profit ₹40 on P and ₹30 on Q. Maximise profit.
cards.definition: Maximise Z = 40x + 30y. Corners: (0, 0) → 0; (0, 80) → 2400; (20, 60) → 2600; (40, 0) → 1600; (40, 20) → 2200. Maximum profit ₹2600 at (20, 60) (20 of P and 60 of Q use exactly the machine time and labour)

cards.term: Diet problem: food X costs ₹5/kg and gives 2 units of vitamin A and 1 of vitamin B; food Y costs ₹4/kg and gives 1 of A and 3 of B. Minimum daily need: 8 units of A and 9 of B. Cheapest mix?
cards.definition: Minimise Z = 5x + 4y subject to 2x + y ≥ 8, x + 3y ≥ 9, x, y ≥ 0 (unbounded region). Corners: (0, 8) → 32; (3, 2) → 23; (9, 0) → 45. The half-plane 5x + 4y < 23 misses the region, so minimum cost ₹23 with 3 kg of X and 2 kg of Y

cards.term: A dealer has ₹15 000 and space for 20 items. A fan costs ₹1500 and yields ₹300 profit; a heater costs ₹500 and yields ₹200. Maximise profit.

A tailor has 24 hours of cutting time and 16 hours of stitching time. A shirt needs 3 h cutting and 2 h stitching (profit ₹30); a trouser needs 4 h cutting and 2 h stitching (profit ₹40). Maximise profit.
cards.definition: Maximise Z = 30x + 40y subject to 3x + 4y ≤ 24, 2x + 2y ≤ 16, x, y ≥ 0. The stitching constraint is redundant. Corners: (0, 0) → 0; (0, 6) → 240; (8, 0) → 240. Maximum ₹240 at (8, 0) and (0, 6), hence at every point of the segment between them (Z = 10(3x + 4y), parallel to the cutting constraint)

cards.term: Multiple optimum test: when is the optimal solution not unique?
cards.definition: When the objective line is parallel to a boundary edge that touches the optimum: the two ends of that edge give equal Z (as in Example 3 and Ex 12.1 Q6–Q8)

cards.term: Iso-profit / iso-cost line method.
cards.definition:
Draw Z = 0 and slide it parallel to itself: the last feasible point it touches (largest c for max, smallest for min) is the optimum.
It is a picture of the corner-point method

cards.term: How do you find corner points quickly?
cards.definition: Intersect pairs of boundary lines (including the axes), then keep only those points that satisfy all the other constraints (the solver above does exactly this)

cards.term: Can the maximum of an LPP occur at an interior point?
cards.definition: No: by Theorem 1 an optimum (if it exists) is at a corner point. For a constant objective (all zero) every point is optimal, but that is not a real LPP

cards.term: What if the objective function is a multiple of one of the constraint lines?
cards.definition: Then there are multiple optimal solutions: the whole edge on that line, from vertex to vertex

cards.term: Does every LPP with a feasible region have a maximum?
cards.definition: No: if the region is unbounded the maximum may not exist (Ex 12.1 Q9). A bounded feasible region always has both max and min

cards.term: How can you check that the LPP has no solution at all?
cards.definition: Look for contradictory constraints (like y ≥ x + 1 and y ≤ x) or plot the half-planes and see that there is no common shaded region

cards.term: Two-phase check for an unbounded minimisation problem.
cards.definition:
Compute Z at the corners and take the smallest m.
Then draw ax + by < m.
If that half-plane misses the region, m is the minimum; otherwise there is no minimum

cards.term: A quick sanity check for a computed optimum.
cards.definition: Substitute the optimum point into every constraint (it must satisfy all of them), then check that Z at neighbouring corners is not better

cards.term:
MCQ: the maximum value of Z = 4x + 3y subject to x + y ≤ 5, x ≤ 3, x, y ≥ 0 is
(a) 15 (b) 18 (c) 17 (d) 12

MCQ: the corner points of a feasible region are (0, 0), (4, 0), (2, 3), (0, 2). Z = 5x + 2y is maximum at
(a) (0, 0) (b) (4, 0) (c) (2, 3) (d) (0, 2)
cards.definition: Z = 0, 20, 16, 4: (b) (4, 0)

cards.term:
MCQ: which is a feasible solution of x + y ≤ 4, x, y ≥ 0?
(a) (3, 2) (b) (1, 2) (c) (5, 0) (d) (−1, 2)
cards.definition: (1, 2): 3 ≤ 4 and non-negative: (b)

cards.term:
MCQ: a feasible region that can be enclosed within a circle is called
(a) bounded (b) unbounded (c) infeasible (d) optimal
cards.definition: (a) bounded

cards.term:
MCQ: the constraints x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 are called
(a) non-negativity restrictions (b) objective function (c) decision variables (d) optimal solutions
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term:
MCQ: if Z = ax + by has the same maximum at two corner points, then
(a) the maximum occurs at every point of the segment joining them (b) no maximum (c) a unique maximum (d) the region is unbounded
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term:
MCQ: the number of corner points of a feasible region defined by x + y ≤ 4, x ≤ 3, x, y ≥ 0 is
(a) 4 (b) 5 (c) 3 (d) 6
cards.definition: Corners (0,0), (3,0), (3,1), (0,4): (a) 4

cards.term: Integer answer (JEE Main): the maximum value of Z = x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 6, x ≤ 4, x, y ≥ 0 is?
Integer answer: the minimum value of Z = 2x + 3y subject to x + y ≥ 5, x ≥ 1, y ≥ 1 is?
cards.definition: Corners (1, 4) and (4, 1) give Z = 14 and 11. The region is unbounded but Z only increases away from the corners: 11

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: the optimal value of an LPP occurs at a corner point of the feasible region.
R: the objective function is linear and the region is convex.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: every LPP with an unbounded feasible region has no maximum.
R: in an unbounded region, values of Z may increase indefinitely.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) A false, R true (c) A true, R false (d) Both false
cards.definition: (b): in an unbounded region a maximum or minimum may or may not exist (Ex 12.1 Q4 has a minimum)

cards.term: True/False: the feasible region of an LPP is always convex.
cards.definition: True

cards.term: True/False: an LPP can have exactly two optimal solutions.
cards.definition: False: two optimal corners force infinitely many optimal points (the whole segment)

cards.term: 2-mark: define feasible region.
cards.definition: The common region determined by all the constraints, including x, y ≥ 0, of a linear programming problem.

cards.term: 3-mark: maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≤ 3, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Corners (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 1), (0, 4): Z = 0, 9, 11, 8. Maximum Z = 11 at (3, 1)

cards.term: 4-mark: a manufacturer makes tables and chairs. A table needs 4 h of carpentry and 2 h of finishing; a chair needs 2 h and 2 h. Available: 40 h carpentry, 30 h finishing. Profit ₹100 per table, ₹60 per chair. Maximise profit.
4-mark: minimise Z = 4x + 3y subject to x + y ≥ 5, 2x + y ≥ 8, x, y ≥ 0.
cards.definition: Corners: (0, 8) → 24; (3, 2) → 18; (5, 0) → 20. The region is unbounded but Z grows in every unbounded direction (the half-plane 4x + 3y < 18 misses it): minimum Z = 18 at (3, 2)

cards.term: Case-based: a farmer has 50 acres and ₹4 000. Wheat costs ₹40/acre and gives ₹200 profit/acre; maize costs ₹100/acre and gives ₹400. How should he plant (fractions of an acre allowed)?
